problem_data.story:
The drilling rig hummed steadily as Pablo Matthews checked the seismic readings one more time. The data streaming across his tablet showed promising geological formations deep beneath the surface of Titan, Saturn's largest moon. Beside him, his wife Valentina Reynolds wiped condensation from her helmet's faceplate, her breath coming in short gasps despite the suit's oxygen regulation.

"We need to keep moving," Pablo said, his voice crackling through the comm system. "The surest way to fail out here is to give up now." He reached over and adjusted the oxygen flow on Valentina's suit, trying to ease her breathing. Through the transparent helmet, he could see exhaustion etched across her features.

She probably blamed him for the rover malfunction, though she hadn't said it outright. Valentina was usually supportive, but when fatigue set in, she could be difficult. It wasn't her fault—anyone would be worn down after twelve hours of trudging across Titan's methane lakes and hydrocarbon dunes.

The rover had died three kilometers back, its drilling mechanism clogged with the moon's thick, viscous hydrocarbons. Some maintenance tech back at the Fairview District base had failed to install the proper filters. But Valentina seemed to think Pablo should have caught the oversight during the pre-mission check.

"Can't we turn back, Pablo?" Valentina pleaded through the comm. "Maybe there aren't any geothermal vents in this sector. This whole expedition feels pointless."

Pablo wanted to remind her that the Geological Survey had specifically directed them to this region, that the systematic observation of Titan's subsurface had indicated significant thermal activity here. But arguing with an exhausted partner never helped.

He stared ahead at the alien landscape. Behind them lay the relative safety of the Fairview District base, ahead only the mysteries of this strange moon's interior. Earth needed the energy—desperately. The Great Collapse of 2087 had devastated the planet's infrastructure when the old power grids failed simultaneously across three continents.

"Try to keep going, Val," he said, using her nickname. "Remember why we're here. We're part of something bigger than ourselves."

She glared at him through her faceplate. "Something bigger? That's easy to say when you're not the one struggling to breathe in this suit. The Geological Survey's compensation is terrible."

"We didn't come for the money, Val."

"I know, but still—"

It had to be hell for her. They'd been searching for geothermal signatures all day, both monitoring the seismic sensors and thermal scanners. The equipment had shown nothing but background readings—the constant low-level thermal activity that meant nothing useful.

Even though Titan's gravity was only a fraction of Earth's, Pablo was starting to tire, and he knew it was worse for Valentina. She was fit, but not engineered for this kind of endurance work.

"Something bigger," she muttered bitterly. "We're not pioneers—we're fools! Why did I let you talk me into joining the Survey Corps?"

Which wasn't remotely accurate. Valentina had been the one to suggest it, inspired by the recruitment campaign after the Great Collapse. They both knew Earth needed new energy sources. The Collapse had happened when someone—no one ever proved who—had deployed an electromagnetic pulse weapon that fried every power station and grid across Asia, Europe, and North America simultaneously. Billions of people had suffered in the aftermath. The world had barely held together.

The recovery had been slow, painful. They'd rebuilt using whatever energy sources they could find: solar, wind, geothermal, fusion where they could manage it. But it wasn't enough. Earth's population needed more power, and the answer lay in the outer solar system—places like Titan, where vast reserves of geothermal energy could be tapped if only they could find the right locations.

Enter the Survey Corps: volunteer teams exploring the outer moons, searching for viable energy extraction sites.

Pablo tried to encourage her. "Buck up. We'll find something soon."

They pressed on across the strange terrain. The thermal scanner maintained its steady baseline reading, never spiking into the dramatic surge that would indicate a major geothermal vent. Pablo felt his own energy flagging. The suit's servo-assists helped, but there were limits.

He looked at Valentina. She was practically sleepwalking now, her movements automatic and uncoordinated.

Twelve steps later, Pablo decided they'd gone far enough for today.

He stopped, removed his scanner harness, and lowered himself to the ground. "What's wrong?" Valentina asked drowsily.

"Nothing. I think we should rest before continuing. It's been a long day."

She didn't need convincing. She slid down beside him, and within moments was asleep, curled up on Titan's frozen surface.

Poor kid, Pablo thought. Maybe they shouldn't have come after all. But someone had to do this work. The Great Collapse had taught humanity that centralized power systems were vulnerable. Three months of chaos had killed millions. The recovery had taken years. They'd rebuilt society with a new understanding: energy independence was survival. But Earth's resources were limited. They needed the outer system.

A second thought appeared: Why us?

He looked at Valentina's sleeping form and thought of their comfortable apartment in Glendale, Xandria, back on Earth. They'd had a good life there—Pablo teaching geology at the university, Valentina working on public health initiatives. But when the recruitment call came, they'd both felt the pull.

The Survey Corps preferred married couples working as teams. It had been the deciding factor. They were a good team, had always been. So they'd volunteered.

And here we are, Pablo thought. The wind—if you could call the methane breeze that—stirred the hydrocarbon sand around them.

He glanced at his suit's chronometer. Getting late. He should wake Valentina. But she looked so peaceful, and he was tired too. So tired. He leaned back against his equipment pack.

He awoke with a start, realizing he'd dozed off. "Come on, Val," he said, moving to stand.

He couldn't.

He looked down. He was wrapped in some kind of polymer restraint, bound from neck to boots, arms pinned, legs trapped. The material was incredibly strong—some kind of advanced smart-polymer that hardened on contact.

It wasn't aliens. There were no aliens on Titan, never had been. It was human work.

He looked at Valentina. She was similarly restrained, still unconscious.

"Val—"

"Don't try to move," said a harsh voice above him. Pablo looked up and saw a figure in an older-model environmental suit. The suit was bulky, outdated by at least twenty years. The helmet was opaque except for the faceplate, through which Pablo could see a weathered face, hard eyes, a grim expression.

The stranger was in a mobility chair—a sophisticated one with all-terrain treads and what looked like a small fusion cell for power. Pablo could see the person had no legs below mid-thigh.

The stranger held a polymer-spray gun in one hand and an energy weapon in the other.

"I've been waiting for you to wake up," the stranger said coldly. "Didn't want to disturb your rest."

Pablo realized with growing horror that this person might have been watching them for hours. The thought sent chills down his spine.

Then anger replaced fear. "What's going on?" Pablo demanded. "Who are you?"

"You'll learn soon enough," came the reply. "For now, you're coming with me." The stranger adjusted the polymer gun's setting and sprayed their legs with a dissolving agent. Their legs were free.

"Stand up. Slowly. Don't try anything foolish." The stranger holstered the polymer gun but kept the energy weapon trained on them.

Pablo and Valentina helped each other up, their arms still bound tightly.

"Walk," the stranger commanded, gesturing with the weapon. "I'll follow."

Pablo could hear the whir of the mobility chair's motors behind them as they walked. He tried to speak to Valentina, but their captor cut him off. "Quiet!"

They trudged forward together, the chair following. Pablo's mind raced. Who was this person? Why were they out here alone? What did they want?

The answer to why they'd come to Titan was clear enough: Earth needed the energy. The Great Collapse had demonstrated how fragile civilization was when power failed. Three months of chaos had killed millions. The recovery had taken years. They'd rebuilt society with a new understanding: energy independence was survival. But Earth's resources were limited. They needed the outer system.

After walking for what felt like an hour, a habitat dome appeared ahead, nestled between two ridges of frozen terrain. It was small—a single-person facility, completely off the grid.

"Welcome to my home," the stranger said. "I'm Ryan Riley." He directed them to the airlock, which responded to his voice commands, and motioned them inside. Once the airlock cycled, he removed his helmet.

His face was bitter, aged beyond its years. This was a person consumed by hatred.

The interior was spartan. No comfort items, no entertainment systems, no decoration. Just the basics: a fabricator for food, a sleeping pod, a work station. And weapons. Several weapons mounted on the walls.

Suddenly Ryan sprayed their legs again with the polymer. They fell heavily to the floor.

"I imagine you want to understand," Ryan said. "The others did too."

Valentina's voice shook. "What others?"

"I never learned their names," Ryan said casually. "Other Survey Corps teams I captured out on the surface. That's my purpose now—hunting surveyors. Look outside."

He gestured through the dome's transparent section. Pablo's stomach turned. There were bones out there—human remains, at least a dozen sets, scattered across the frozen ground. Remnants of environmental suits clung to them.

Pablo suddenly remembered. There had been disappearances. The Survey Corps didn't talk about it much, attributing the losses to the hazardous environment. But there had been a pattern. Six, eight, maybe ten names he could recall. None had been close friends—you didn't have time to make close friends out here. But they'd all promised themselves it wouldn't happen to them.

It had.

"You've been hunting surveyors?" Pablo asked. "Why? What have we done to you?"

Ryan smiled coldly. "Because I hate you all. I intend to eliminate every surveyor, one by one, until your organization abandons Titan."

Pablo stared. He'd never encountered hatred this pure before.

"He's insane!" Valentina said.

"No," Ryan replied evenly. "I'm quite sane. But I'm determined to drive the Survey Corps off Titan. Eventually, you'll all leave."

"By picking us off one by one?"

"Exactly. And don't think about armed retaliation. This facility is well-defended. I've spent years building it. I'm protected by these ridges. They can't reach me."

"What are you going to do with us?" Valentina finally asked.

"Kill her," Ryan said, nodding at Valentina. "You, I'll send back as a messenger. To tell the others to leave Titan."

He rocked slightly in his chair, the energy weapon steady in his hand.

It was a nightmare. Pablo frantically searched for options.

"Do I shock you?" Ryan asked. "I shouldn't—not when you understand my motives."

"We don't understand," Pablo snapped.

"Then let me explain. You're on Titan searching for geothermal energy sites, correct? To establish extraction operations and send power back to Earth. Right?"

Pablo nodded.

"We volunteered," Valentina said quietly.

"Ah, two young heroes," Ryan said with acid sarcasm. "How noble. I might pity you. Almost."

"What do you want?" Pablo said, trying to buy time.

"The Great Collapse cost me my legs," Ryan said. "You remember the Victorville Incident?"

"Of course." Everyone remembered. When the electromagnetic pulse hit, Victorville in Thandor had been conducting experimental fusion research. The power surge from the EMP had caused a catastrophic containment failure. Hundreds dead, thousands injured, an entire region contaminated.

"I was there as a consultant," Ryan said. "I represented Riley Energy Systems. I was there to finalize a contract. You know who I am now?"

Pablo nodded slowly, recognition dawning.

"I was partially shielded when it happened. I didn't get the contract, but I got a massive dose of radiation. Not enough to kill me," he said. "Just enough to require amputation." He indicated his missing legs. "So I was lucky."

Pablo still didn't understand. "But why kill us? We had nothing to do with Victorville."

"You're collateral damage," Ryan said. "After the incident and the amputation, my partners at Riley Energy Systems decided a disabled CEO was bad for business. They forced me out. All legal, I assure you. They left me with almost nothing."

Then he delivered the punchline.

"They renamed the company. Who did you say you worked for?"

Pablo began, "The Geological Sur—"

"Don't bother. They bought out three smaller operations and rebranded. Riley Energy Systems became the Geological Survey Corporation. More professional-sounding, wouldn't you say?" He grinned humorlessly. "I saved for years, came to Titan, built this facility, and swore revenge. There's significant geothermal potential on this moon, but I'll make sure your company never exploits it."

He checked his chronometer. "Time for my medication." He sprayed them again with polymer for security, then rolled to a medical station and retrieved a hypospray. "Another souvenir of Victorville. I need regular injections—immunosuppressants, pain management, others. The radiation turned me into a medical dependent. But I'll make them all pay."

Pablo's mind raced. The situation was nightmarish—not just the immediate danger, but the twisted psychology behind it. How could a human mind become this warped?

He saw the horror on Valentina's face and knew she felt the same.

"Do you really think you can succeed?" Pablo challenged him. "Really think you can kill every surveyor on Titan? Of all the insane—"

Valentina's warning look cut him off, but Ryan had already reacted.

"Yes! I'll make them pay for taking my legs! If we hadn't meddled with fusion power in the first place, I'd be whole today—instead of a cripple in this chair."

"You're sick, Ryan Riley," Valentina said quietly. "You've created an impossible revenge fantasy and now you're taking it out on innocent people who've done nothing to you. That's not sane."

His eyes blazed. "Who are you to judge sanity?"

Pablo caught Valentina's glance. Sweat beaded on her forehead despite the suit's climate control.

"Why don't you do something?" she whispered urgently. "What are you waiting for?"

"Easy," Pablo said softly. He knew their advantage. But he needed Ryan closer.

"Enough," Ryan said. "I'm going to release you outside, right after—"

"Get sick!" Pablo hissed to Valentina. She immediately began coughing violently, gasping and writhing in her restraints. "Can't breathe!" she yelled.

Ryan hesitated. Despite everything, some humanity remained. He lowered the energy weapon slightly and rolled closer to examine Valentina. She continued her convincing performance, retching and moaning.

Ryan approached and leaned down to look at her. He opened his mouth to speak, and Pablo snapped his leg up hard, breaking through the polymer restraint with a sharp crack, and kicked the mobility chair over.

The energy weapon discharged, burning a hole through the dome's wall. Emergency sealant deployed instantly. Ryan sprawled on the floor, the chair overturned beside him, wheels spinning uselessly. The weapon flew from his hands and slid across the floor near Pablo.

In one motion, Pablo rolled and covered the weapon with his body.

Ryan dragged himself toward Pablo with desperate effort, trying to pry the weapon free, but Pablo twisted and kicked him away. Ryan hit the wall and lay there, stunned.

Valentina rolled closer. "Now we just need to get free of this polymer," Pablo said.

"Teamwork," Valentina replied. She maneuvered until her head was near Pablo's hands. "Can you reach the release tab on my helmet?"

Pablo's fingers, clumsy in the restraints, fumbled for the helmet's emergency release. Finally, he found it and triggered it. The helmet's seal broke with a hiss.

"There," she breathed.

Pablo glanced at Ryan, who was groaning and beginning to stir.

Valentina positioned her face near Pablo's bound arms and began working at the polymer with her teeth, gnawing at it until it started to separate. One strand broke, then another. Finally, Pablo had enough mobility to grasp the weapon.

He pulled himself across the floor to Ryan, located the polymer gun, and dissolved the remaining restraints. His muscles were stiff and protesting as he stood. He freed Valentina, then turned to face Ryan.

"I suppose you'll kill me now," Ryan said.

"No," Pablo told him. "That's the difference between sane people and the insane. I'm not going to kill you. I'm going to ensure you're sent back to Earth."

"No!" Ryan shouted. "Not back there! I can't face them again—not after what they did—"

"Not so loud," Pablo interrupted. "They'll help you on Earth. They have treatments now—psychological rehabilitation, conflict resolution therapy. They'll treat the hatred and trauma, help you become functional again."

"I hate them all," Ryan spat.

"I know," Pablo said. "You're consumed by hate. You hated Earth so much that you couldn't stay there even six months after Victorville. You had to flee to Titan immediately, didn't you? Your hate was so overwhelming you had to run."

"Why are you saying this?"

"Because if you'd stayed longer, you'd have learned about the Victorville Response Initiative. The public health programs that came out of the Collapse."

Ryan scowled, then his expression turned defiant. "They told me I was paralyzed. That I'd never walk again, even with prosthetics, because the nerve damage was too severe."

"You left Earth too quickly," Valentina said gently.

"It was the only way," Ryan protested. "I had to escape—"

"She's right," Pablo told him. "Medical science advanced rapidly after the Collapse. The crisis forced innovation—neural-interface prosthetics, cybernetic limbs with direct brain control. All the Victorville survivors received them, free of charge, as part of the public health response. All except you. You were so consumed by hate that you fled before you could benefit."

"You're lying," Ryan said weakly. "It's not possible. That technology didn't exist before the Collapse."

"Correct," Pablo said. "It didn't. The crisis created the need, and the need drove the breakthrough. Millions of survivors needed prosthetics, rehabilitation, medical care. The old systems couldn't cope. So they built new ones."

"Neural-interface technology was theoretical before 2087," Valentina added. "The Collapse changed everything. Suddenly there was funding, urgency, desperation. What might have taken decades happened in months."

Ryan's face contorted with confusion and rage. "So you're saying the Collapse... helped people?"

"Helped some. Devastated others," Pablo said carefully. "It's complicated. The point is, you could have been helped. You chose not to be."

"Haven't you wondered how I broke through the polymer restraints when I kicked your chair?" Pablo asked.

"Yes—human legs aren't strong enough for that."

"Correct," Pablo said. He signaled Valentina to keep the weapon trained on Ryan while he opened his suit's leg panels. "Look," he said, revealing the gleaming cybernetic limbs beneath. The soft hum of their servomotors was barely audible. "I was at Victorville too. But I didn't let hatred consume me when I lost my legs."

Ryan stared at the prosthetics, then at Pablo's face. "You... you were there?"

"Teaching assistant at the university. I was in the city for a conference when the EMP hit and the containment failed. Lost both legs below the knee." Pablo's voice was steady. "I spent eight months in rehabilitation. Watched them develop the neural-interface technology in real-time, practically. First-generation prototypes were crude. By the time I was fitted, they were already on the third iteration."

"The technology developed in response to the Collapse," Valentina said. "It wasn't a silver lining—that would be obscene to say. But it was something that came after, because of the need."

Ryan was sobbing now. "I didn't know. I couldn't have known."

"You could have," Pablo said quietly. "If you'd stayed. If you'd let yourself be helped instead of running."

"But the EMP—the Collapse—it destroyed everything—"

"The EMP caused the Collapse," Valentina said. "What came after was different. Recovery. Adaptation. Some things got worse. Some things, unexpectedly, got better. The prosthetics program was one of the better things."

"Okay, Ryan," Pablo said. Valentina helped him into his helmet. "Get your helmet secured and let's go. Between the psychological rehabilitation and the prosthetics specialists, you'll be a different person within a year."

"But I'm a murderer!"

"That's right. You'll be sentenced to rehabilitative therapy. When they're finished, Ryan Riley the killer will be gone, but there'll be a new, healthy Ryan Riley." Pablo turned to Valentina. "Got the scanners?"

For the first time since their capture, Pablo remembered how exhausted Valentina had been. He realized he'd been pushing her too hard—him with his cybernetic legs and enhanced endurance. No wonder she'd been ready to collapse. And he'd been too focused on the mission to notice.

She lifted the scanner harnesses, and Pablo helped Ryan back into his chair.

Valentina resealed her helmet.

"Let's get back to Fairview District quickly," Pablo said. "We'll turn Ryan over to the authorities. Then we can catch the next transport to Earth."

"Go back? Go back?" Valentina's voice was incredulous. "If you think I'm quitting now, you're crazy! After we hand this guy over, I'm sleeping for twenty hours, and then we're going back out there to finish our survey pattern. Earth needs those geothermal sites, and I know you'd never be happy leaving the job half-done." She smiled. "I can't wait to get back out there and find those thermal signatures."

Pablo laughed with relief and hugged her carefully through their suits. When he released her, she squeezed his gloved hand.

"Let's move, fellow pioneer," she said.

Pablo activated the airlock controls, smiling despite everything. They had work to do.
